# Written Report 1: Overview and Design

## Row {data-height="360"}

### Report Purpose

:::: report-card
::: callout-title
What this report explains
:::

This written report summarizes the purpose, data preparation, dashboard design, key findings, recommendations, and limitations for the Superstore Sales Performance Dashboard.
::::

### How to Read the Dashboard

::: key-point
Start with the **Overall Summary** to understand overall sales, profit, orders, and profit margin. Then move through product, geography, and customer sections to identify what is driving those results. 
:::

## Row {data-height="360"}

### 1. Data Source and Description

::: report-card
The dashboard uses the updated Excel workbook \*\*sample\_-\_superstore.xls\*\*.

The dashboard reads the **Orders** sheet because it contains the transaction-level fields needed for business analysis, including:

<ul class="report-list">

<li><strong>Dates:</strong> Order Date and Ship Date</li>

<li><strong>Financial measures:</strong> Sales, Profit, Discount, and Quantity</li>

<li><strong>Customer information:</strong> Segment and Ship Mode</li>

<li><strong>Product information:</strong> Category and Sub-Category</li>

<li><strong>Geography:</strong> Region and State/Province</li>

</ul>

This dataset works well for a dashboard because it connects financial outcomes with products, customers, and locations.
:::

### 2. Data Preparation and Accuracy

:::: report-card
Before visualization, the data are cleaned and prepared so the charts are accurate.

<ul class="report-list">

<li>The Orders sheet is imported from the Excel workbook.</li>

<li>Order Date and Ship Date are converted into proper date variables.</li>

<li>Sales, Profit, Quantity, and Discount are converted into numeric variables.</li>

<li>Profit Margin is calculated as Profit divided by Sales.</li>

<li>A monthly date variable is created from Order Date.</li>

<li>Rows with missing Order Date, Sales, or Profit are removed.</li>

</ul>

::: success-point
<strong>Important accuracy update:</strong> The monthly trend chart now groups orders by month before plotting sales and profit. This means each point represents a true monthly total.
:::
::::

## Row {data-height="410"}

### 3. Monthly Trend Logic

::: report-card
The monthly sales and profit trend uses the following logic:

```{r written-monthly-trend-example, eval=FALSE}
trend_data <- filtered_data() %>%
  mutate(Month = floor_date(Order_Date, "month")) %>%
  group_by(Month) %>%
  summarise(
    Sales = sum(Sales, na.rm = TRUE),
    Profit = sum(Profit, na.rm = TRUE),
    Orders = n_distinct(Order_ID),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Each row in `trend_data` represents one month. This prevents the dashboard from incorrectly plotting individual transactions as monthly values.
:::

### 4. Dashboard Organization

::: report-card
The dashboard is organized so users can move from broad performance to detailed exploration.

<ol class="report-list">

<li><strong>Dashboard Summary:</strong> KPIs and monthly sales/profit trends.</li>

<li><strong>Product Performance:</strong> product categories and sub-categories.</li>

<li><strong>Geographic Analysis:</strong> states, provinces, and regions.</li>

<li><strong>Customer Insights:</strong> customer segments and shipping methods.</li>

<li><strong>Data Explorer:</strong> searchable and downloadable filtered data.</li>

</ol>
:::

# Written Report 2: Findings and Recommendations

## Row {data-height="390"}

### 5. Key Findings

:::: report-card
The dashboard is designed to reveal several practical insights:

<ul class="report-list">

<li>Monthly sales and profit can be compared to identify seasonal patterns.</li>

<li>High sales do not always mean high profit.</li>

<li>Some categories and sub-categories may require pricing or discount review.</li>

<li>Regional and state-level charts help identify stronger and weaker markets.</li>

<li>Customer segment analysis helps show which customer groups drive revenue.</li>

</ul>

::: warning-point
The most important interpretation is to compare **sales and profit together**. A business area with high sales but low profit may need closer review.
:::
::::

### 6. Recommendations

::: report-card
Based on the dashboard design and the types of insights it supports, Superstore should:

<ul class="report-list">

<li>Track monthly sales and profit together instead of focusing only on revenue.</li>

<li>Investigate high-sales areas with low or negative profit.</li>

<li>Review discounts in low-profit categories and sub-categories.</li>

<li>Focus marketing and inventory planning on profitable regions and segments.</li>

<li>Use filters to compare performance across time, products, customers, and geography.</li>

</ul>
:::

## Row {data-height="360"}

### 7. Limitations

::: report-card
The dashboard is useful for exploration, but it has limits.

<ul class="report-list">

<li>The data are historical and do not prove causation.</li>

<li>The dashboard does not include every possible business cost.</li>

<li>Profit results depend on the accuracy of the profit field in the dataset.</li>

<li>Some patterns may be affected by discounts, shipping, or business rules not fully shown in the data.</li>

<li>The dashboard does not forecast future sales or profit.</li>

</ul>
:::

### 8. Conclusion

::: report-card
The dashboard provides a clear and interactive view of the Superstore performance. It combines KPIs, monthly sales and profit trends, product analysis, geographic comparisons, customer insights, and a searchable data table to analyze performace in the store. 
:::
